questions.question: Write the fraction 7/10 as a decimal.
questions.explain: Tenths go in the first place after the decimal point, so 7/10 = 0.7. A common trap is writing 0.07 — that is 7 hundredths, which means the whole was cut into 100 equal parts, not 10.

questions.question: Which decimal is equal to 43/100?
questions.explain: Hundredths need two places after the decimal point, so 43 hundredths is 0.43. Students often slide the digits over and write 0.043 or 4.3; count the places instead — the last digit must land in the hundredths place.

questions.question: In the number 0.36, what is the value of the digit 6?
questions.explain: Reading right from the decimal point, the first place is tenths (3 tenths) and the second is hundredths, so the 6 means 6 hundredths. The trap is naming the place by the digit's size instead of its position.

questions.question: A hundred grid is one whole, and it is cut into 100 equal squares. Exactly 9 squares are coloured. Which decimal shows the coloured part?
questions.explain: Each small square is 1 hundredth, so 9 squares is 9/100 = 0.09. Writing 0.9 is the usual slip — that would be 9 whole columns of the grid, ten times as much.

questions.question: At the school store, Ravi buys an eraser for 8 cents. Which choice shows 8 cents as a part of one dollar?
questions.explain: One dollar is 100 equal cents, so 8 cents is 8/100 = $0.08. Many students write $0.8 or $0.80, but that is 8 dimes — always fill the hundredths place when writing cents.

questions.question: Three schools measured the snow on their fields: Maple School 0.3 m, Cedar School 0.25 m, Birch School 0.09 m. Which list puts the depths in order from least to greatest?
questions.explain: Give every number the same number of places first: 0.30, 0.25, 0.09, so the order is 0.09 < 0.25 < 0.30. The classic trap is thinking 0.25 beats 0.3 because 25 is bigger than 3 — compare tenths first, not the number of digits.

questions.question: For an art project, Ella colours 4 full columns of a hundred grid (4 tenths) and then 7 more single squares (7 hundredths). What decimal shows how much of the grid she has coloured?
questions.explain: Tenths go in the first place and hundredths in the second, so 4 tenths and 7 hundredths make 0.47 (that's 47 of the 100 squares). Don't add 4 + 7 to get 0.11, and don't stack the numbers side by side as 0.407 — each digit needs its own place.

questions.question: A community garden bed is divided into 100 equal squares. Owen has planted 0.3 of the bed. How many squares has he planted?
questions.explain: 0.3 = 3 tenths = 30/100, so 30 of the 100 squares are planted. Reading 0.3 as "3 squares" is the common mistake — 3 squares would be 0.03 of the bed.

questions.question: In gym class Kai ran 0.45 km and Sofia ran 0.5 km. Kai says he ran farther because 45 is bigger than 5. Who actually ran farther, and why?
options: Kai, because 0.45 has more digits than 0.5.
Sofia, because 0.5 is the same as 0.50, and 50 hundredths is more than 45 hundredths.
They tied, because both distances are less than 1 km.
Kai, because 45 hundredths is more than 5 hundredths.
questions.explain: Write both to hundredths first: 0.5 = 0.50 and 0.50 > 0.45, so Sofia ran farther. The most common decimal mistake is thinking a longer decimal is a bigger number — adding a zero to the end of 0.5 does not change its value.

questions.question: Ben buys a bookmark for $0.35 and pays with a loonie ($1.00). What fraction of a dollar does he get back in change?
questions.explain: First find the change: $1.00 − $0.35 = $0.65, then write it over 100 because a dollar has 100 cents, giving 65/100. Watch two traps — writing the price instead of the change, and dropping the last cent to get 6/10 ($0.60).

questions.question: Mrs. Chen's class garden bed is 100 equal squares. Carrots fill 0.4 of the bed, and peas fill 15 squares. What decimal shows the part of the bed that is still empty?
questions.explain: Change 0.4 into squares first: 0.4 = 40 squares, so 40 + 15 = 55 squares are planted and 100 − 55 = 45 squares are empty, which is 0.45. The trap is adding 4 + 15 without converting the tenths into hundredths.

questions.question: At the corner store, Leo pays with 4 dimes and 3 pennies. Leo writes the amount as $0.43, his sister writes it as 43/100 of a dollar, and their friend writes it as 4/10 + 3/100 of a dollar. Which statement is true?
options: Only Leo is right, because money cannot be written as a fraction.
Only Leo and his sister are right, because 4/10 + 3/100 equals 0.043.
No one is right, because 4 dimes and 3 pennies is $4.30.
All three are right, because they all name 43 hundredths of a dollar.
questions.explain: Each dime is 1 tenth of a dollar and each penny is 1 hundredth, so 4/10 + 3/100 = 0.40 + 0.03 = 0.43 = 43/100 — the same amount written three ways. The trap is thinking a decimal and a fraction must be different numbers, or lining up the coin digits as $4.30.
